Deliberately we_write = false. A superfloppy is defined by the ABSENCE of a
partition table, so there is nothing for an oracle to inspect — any filesystem
oracle that reads the volume at offset 0 has already proved it. Listing it as
a write path would manufacture a permanent unfillable gap.

Measured 2026-08-07 on macOS 26.5.2 (fsck_hfs hfs-715.120.4): it still checks

Both were also confirmed against Mac OS X 10.5.8 on a PowerMac G5, which

SGI IRIS 3130 (68020) emulator, booting the real IRIX 3.7 / GL2-W3.6
disk to a shell. The counterpart to `iris`, one machine generation earlier: iris
checks IRIX EFS on an Indy, motion checks EFS **v1** on the hardware that
format was written for.

Its serial console goes to stdout, one line per `[Emulation - Serial] ... [line
1] <text>`, so a whole boot is greppable with no X, no xdotool and no screen
scraping. Run it WITHOUT `+set enableGF2 1`; the graphics console needs XTEST
typing and is useless for CI. It needs assets/ roms/ profile/ beside the
binary — symlinks are fine — and reads the disk from `profile/3130.img`.

The check drives a guest script instead of a control socket: the volume under
test is dropped into the reference disk's /usr slot, /etc/rc.s0 is patched to
mount /dev/md0c and list it, and the console is the verdict. Word order is
load-bearing — the medium is swapped within every 16-bit word, so the check
swab16s a natively-written volume on the way in.

Four things that cost time:

  * It opens the disk READ-ONLY and only ever attaches drive 0 (dsd5217.cpp
    calls Profile::OpenDisk(0) and nothing else). `profileDisk1Path` exists but
    is unwired, so "attach our whole disk as md1" does not work yet — hence the
    splice into an existing slot.
  * About one boot in six dies at kernel entry before running anything. That is
    the emulator, not the volume, so the check retries once and reports exit 99
    (no verdict) rather than inventing a finding.
  * `/mnt` does not exist on the reference disk. Without `mkdir` the mount
    fails in a way that reads like a filesystem fault.
  * IRIX 3.7's mount is silent on success. Its refusal is
    "/dev/md0c:Invalid argument", not anything with "mount:" in it — matching
    the wrong string is how a broken volume passes.

Control, run 2026-08-24: 8 MB of urandom in the same slot yields
"/dev/md0c:Invalid argument" and exit 1, so a pass is not the check passing
everything.

`scripts/sgi-efs-v1-oracle.sh prove` is the deeper, standalone form: it has
rb-cli rewrite-and-grow /etc/rc.s0, create a file and a directory and allocate
a 256 KiB file on the reference disk itself, then boots and confirms IRIX runs
the script, reads them back and `sum`s to the right checksum. Not wired to an
artifact, so it is not a `check`; it is what a person runs after touching the
write path.

SGI Indy (MIPS R4400) emulator with a purpose-built CI control
socket: `iris-ci` has put / run / get / snapshot-rollback, and `run` returns the
guest's stdout — no screen-scraping at all.

Brought up 2026-08-12, as far as a live IRIX shell:

  IRIS_JIT=1 iris --headless --noaudio --ci --scsi1 disks/Indy-IRIX65_dev.chd --cdrom4 <any.iso>
  iris-ci boot && iris-ci login && iris-ci run "uname -aR"
    -> IRIX IRIS 6.5 6.5.22m 10070055 IP22

Four things that cost time, recorded so they do not again:

  * No PROM needed. It warns about a missing prom.bin and uses an embedded one.
    Do not go hunting for Indy firmware.
  * --ci is required for the control socket. Without it iris listens only on
    the monitor port 8888 and iris-ci cannot reach 19851.
  * A CD-ROM must be attached even when booting from disk, or startup dies with
    "could not attach cdrom4.iso". Any ISO will do.
  * IRIX 6.5 boots; the 5.3 image hangs. Indy-IRIX53_dev.chd reaches "The
    system is coming up", prints "Find Error: 10" and never reaches a login
    prompt. Indy-IRIX65_dev.chd reaches one in a few minutes with JIT on.

SOLVED 2026-08-13. The scratch volume is configured in iris.toml, not on the
command line — --help never mentions it, but the binary does: "set
`scratch = true` on a SCSI device in iris.toml". `scsi` is a MAP keyed by id,
not an array of tables, and every device needs `cdrom`. iris creates the
scratch volume itself, SGI volume header and all:

  [scsi.1]
  path = "disks/Indy-IRIX65_dev.chd"
  cdrom = false

  [scsi.2]
  path = "disks/scratch.img"
  cdrom = false
  scratch = true
  size_mb = 64

Then `iris-ci put <file> --to /tmp/x` stages through it and works.

fsck needs one step more. IRIX refuses a plain file — "Can't find equivalent
raw device" — exactly as macOS fsck_hfs does. But the scratch volume IS a real
SCSI disk in the guest, so write the image straight into it and check the
device node:

  iris-ci scratch write ./volume.img
  iris-ci run "/sbin/fsck -t efs -n /dev/rdsk/dks0d2s0 < /dev/null"

SCSI id 2 is dks0d2, s0 is the payload partition. The `< /dev/null` matters:
without it fsck waits on a SALVAGE prompt forever.

First result: our EFS volume passes phases 1-4 and fails phase 5 with BAD FREE

--nfs-dir was tried first and abandoned. iris exports the directory fine but
the guest cannot mount it ("Port mapper failure"), then loops retrying and

A headless, CLI-driven Amiga emulator in Rust, and the first
emulator oracle `verify` can actually run. FS-UAE and WinUAE are the same
emulator family and both need a hand-configured guest, so their pairs resolve
to skip-manual; Copperline runs unthrottled with no window, exits on its own
via `--screenshot-after`, and takes its whole machine from a config file.

The AFFS check is a real mount verdict: a Kickstart 3.1 guest mounts the
artifact as DH1: beside a bootable Workbench on DH0 and reports `Info` over
the serial line, which Copperline bridges to its own stdout — no results
volume, no sentinel poll. `attach_check.py` remains for formats with no
guest-side probe yet; it covers the container and the boot block, not the
attach path classifies an image and reads its dostype before any ROM runs, so
a second implementation confirms the bytes we wrote there. Mounting the volume
would need a guest OS, which means a licensed Kickstart plus a Workbench; the
oracle's README has the shape that takes. Scored `smoke` accordingly — it is
not evidence the filesystem is correct.

It boots Copperline's own AROS ROM rather than a Kickstart, so no host needs a
licensed ROM to run it. `program` is python3 on the amitools pattern: the
interpreter is what must exist, and the script finds the emulator (sibling
checkout, or $COPPERLINE).

`program` is python3, not fs-uae: the check is a wrapper script, so
the interpreter is what must be executable. The script finds the emulator
itself and exits 77 (skip-unavailable) when it or a Kickstart is missing,
which is the only way a script-based check can say "not installed here"
rather than reporting a FAIL against our bytes.

Built 2026-08-14 as `oracles/fsuae/affs_mount.py`: it unpacks the Workbench
fixture to a host directory for DH0, writes the probe into its
S/Startup-Sequence, generates the config, launches FS-UAE, polls for the

Working end to end 2026-08-14: it answered R-020. Kickstart 3.1 mounts our AFFS

The one trap, because it cost an afternoon and looks like an emulator fault:
the guest script must be written with LF endings, in bytes. Python's
write_text applies the platform newline on Windows, AmigaDOS scripts are
LF-terminated, and the guest then read a redirect whose target ended in a
carriage return — an
illegal filename on the host directory DH2 maps to. Every redirect failed,
FAILAT 21 stopped the script aborting, and the run booted and silently
produced nothing.

amitools' xdftool — a pure-Python AmigaDOS filesystem reader, and the

Not authoritative: it is a reimplementation, so it agreeing does not prove a
real Amiga will mount the volume, and it disagreeing does not prove one will
not. What it does give is a second implementation reading the same bytes, which
is exactly what R-020 lacked — every AFFS check until now was our own code
agreeing with itself.

Two quirks that cost an afternoon if unknown. It picks its geometry from the
file EXTENSION: a 2 MB volume named `.adf` is rejected as an invalid floppy
size, and must be `.hdf` to be read as a hard-disk volume. And it opens
read-write by default, so a read-only artifact fails with EACCES before it
parses anything — `-r` does not help, because the open happens first.

Confirmed 2026-08-07. The project is real and active: github.com/twvd/snow,
MIT, Linux/macOS/Windows, hardware-level 68000/020/030 emulation of the 128K
through SE/30, with SCSI hard disk and CD support. The 2026-08-02 HTTP 403 was
snowemu.com blocking the fetch, not a dead project.

Its automation surface is the open question, and the answer is "not directly".
There is no CLI frontend — `frontend_egui` is the only one. The `testrunner`
crate IS headless (clap, PNG/GIF output, parallel), but it is built for Snow's
own emulation-accuracy suite: `single` takes a ROM, a floppy image, a recorded
input replay and a control *frame*, boots, and image-diffs the framebuffer.
Repurposing that as a format oracle means authoring an input replay and a
known-good screenshot per format, and supplying Mac ROMs. Possible, but a
project rather than a check command, and brittle in a way a fsck is not.

So: keep it registered as the emulator oracle of record for MFS, but do not
plan on automating it soon. For classic HFS an older macOS with a real
HFS-Standard-capable fsck_hfs is far cheaper and equally authoritative.

For our own container formats there is no third party and never will
be, so structural inspection is circular by construction. The honest check is
behavioural: back up a real installed system, restore it, and boot the result.
If the machine still comes up and its files are intact, the format did its job.

Canonical scenario, which also exercises CB-DOS end to end:

  1. Build a small DOS 6.22 VM (QEMU or VMware) and install it bootable.
  2. Back that disk up with rb-cli into cbk.
  3. Restore onto an SD card (or back into a VM disk).
  4. Boot it and assert the guest reaches a prompt with its files intact.

This single case covers more than the container: backup, restore, the CB-DOS
path, partition and boot-sector fidelity, and — when the target is real media
— the hardware write path from HARDWARE.md. Highest coverage-per-case in the
suite, which is why it is worth the setup cost.
